_readme: Replay season (coaching-quality 05): a beginner's first block, metric, with four hard weeks, each marked by a `_note` the script ignores and the model never sees. Fictional athlete, race and places. Regenerate with `npx tsx scripts/regenerate-replay-seasons.ts` from api/ (see tests/fixtures/README.md).

athlete.name: Nessa Dorrington
athlete.story: A first block from no running, walk-run three mornings a week towards a first 5K: a fever in week 3, a week of nothing in week 5, and two missed weeks for a family reason in weeks 7 and 8.

aboutYou:
# About you

You are new to running. You started in late August, at 41, to get fitter, and want to run the whole of the Corrowmore Harvest 5K on Sunday 15 November without walking. You run three mornings a week (Monday, Wednesday and Saturday), walk-run for now, and walk the dog most days. You have not run since school. No injuries.

weeks._note: Hard week (first week): three 20 to 24 minute walk-runs, about 8 km, the only week of history there is; the athlete asks to run every day to be ready sooner. A careless plan jumps to daily running or longer sessions with nothing to judge it against. The volume jump rule is not skipped, which is itself a finding: the report shows the weeks before as 0.00 km, so the rule judges against a quarter of this one week (1.7 km) and trips on any plan in distance above about 2.3 km, careful or not, while a plan in minutes counts as no distance and trips nothing; long-run jump judges against the one longest run (2.6 km). A careful coach says no to daily running, keeps three days with rest between, and moves on by a small step (a little more running in each repeat).

weekly.body_check: Calves tight the day after each run, gone by the next morning
questions_for_coach: I want to be ready for the 5K in November. Should I run every day next week to get there faster?

weekly.feeling_into_next_week: Good, the two-minute runs were hard but I did them

weeks._note: Hard week (illness): a cold that became a fever (38.4 C) on Tuesday; one of three walk-runs done, still coughing; the athlete asks to make up the two missed runs. No rule covers illness yet (the coach may add one); a careless plan that adds the missed runs to next week trips volume jump only if it is written in distance, since a plan in minutes counts as no distance. A careful coach rests the athlete until the fever has been gone a few days and the chest is clear, then restarts a step back (the week-2 walk-run), says not to make up runs, and says when to see a doctor.

weeks._note: Hard week (nothing run, feeling fine): three walk-runs planned, none run, and a cheerful check-in that gives no reason. A careful coach asks what got in the way, without judgement, and repeats the last week that was run (week 4) rather than moving on.

weeks._note: Hard week (two missed weeks): the plan stood for two weeks running and nothing was run, for a family reason given in both check-ins; the race is four weeks away and the athlete asks whether to start again from the beginning. A careless plan resumes where the plan left off or adds runs to catch up; volume jump judges against a recent average near zero, so almost any plan written in distance trips it, careful or not, a catch-up plan with a longer run also trips long-run jump, and a plan in minutes alone trips nothing. A careful coach is kind about the reason, restarts a step back (the week-4 walk-run), and is honest that the 5K may include some walking, which is fine for a first race.
